images.caption: The African Burial Ground National Monument is the final resting place of approximately 15,000 African New Yorkers. In use until 1794, it was the holiest place in New York for men and women of African descent. It was rediscovered during construction of a federal office building in 1991 and is regarded as the most important urban archaeological discovery of the twentieth century. The African Burial Ground was designated a National Historic Landmark by the Secretary of the Interior in 1993, and it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
images.alt: The African Burial Ground National Monument is the final resting place of approximately 15,000 African New Yorkers. In use until 1794, it was the holiest place in New York for men and women of African descent. It was rediscovered during construction of a federal office building in 1991 and is regarded as the most important urban archaeological discovery of the twentieth century. The African Burial Ground was designated a National Historic Landmark by the Secretary of the Interior in 1993, and it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

images.filename: "A Law for Regulating Negro's & Slaves in the Night Time" (bc676864-1dd8-b71b-0b73-8be3d2e52694).jpg
images.caption:
"A Law for Regulating Negro's & Slaves in the Night Time"
The New York Common Council enacted an ordinance providing "that no Negro, Mullato or Indian Slave, shall appear in the Streets of this City, above an hour after Sun-set without a candle and Lanthorn, on penalty of being Whipt at the Publick Whipping Post."
